repository.name: emhass
repository.title: Home Energy Automation Lab
repository.description: Study home-energy optimization and EV charging windows through practical lessons that retain upstream EMHASS interfaces.
repository.summary: This fork preserves EMHASS energy optimization, forecasts, and Home Assistant interfaces. A synthetic EV charging exercise explains energy windows and the distinction between a planner and a device executor.
repository.audience: Home-energy developers, automation learners, and contributors studying deferrable-load planning.

model.equation: P = charger · efficiency; charge is linear to 80%, then the remaining 20% follows an exponential taper with time constant 0.2Q/P hours.
assumptions: Constant input power until 80% charge, followed by a continuous exponential taper.
Charging begins below 80%; efficiency is constant and the battery is at ideal temperature.
No charger handshake, grid constraint, degradation, or real vehicle data is represented.
The source remains a fork of davidusb-geek/emhass with David HERNANDEZ TORRES and contributor attribution preserved.
Native EV documentation describes a windowed deferrable energy load; the browser taper is an additional illustrative physical assumption, not the native optimizer.
No vehicle, tariff, forecast provider, energy meter, or evcc service is connected; the lesson is entirely offline.
model.introduction: The browser integrates an invented charging curve with constant efficiency and a taper above 80% SOC. It does not run EMHASS, schedule tariffs, call Home Assistant, or send commands to a charger.

modules.title: Translate a charging target into stored energy
modules.objective: Relate battery capacity, charge efficiency, power, and a fixed time window.
steps: Read the EV study case and identify the difference between kW, kWh, and a departure deadline.
Apply a 60 kWh battery at 20% SOC, a 10 kW charger, and 90% efficiency.
Predict stored energy after two hours before running the synthetic curve.
modules.reflection: Why should an optimizer distinguish energy supplied by a charger from energy actually stored in the battery?

modules.title: Check the time-window calculation
modules.objective: Determine whether a nominal charging target is reachable within a stated window.
steps: Keep the 60 kWh battery and 20% initial SOC.
Increase charger power to 20 kW at 90% efficiency and calculate when 80% SOC is reached.
Run to 120 minutes and compare the result with the deferrable-load energy/deadline inputs described in the source.

checkpoints.label: SOC reaches the taper boundary at 80%

modules.reflection: Which runtime fields would a real integration need to keep up to date, and which device-specific measurements are absent here?

modules.title: Expose the constant-power approximation
modules.objective: Explain how a physical charging taper changes a naive energy-over-power estimate.
steps: Start the 60 kWh battery at 50% SOC with the 20 kW charger and 90% efficiency.
Predict when the 80% boundary occurs and why power then declines in this toy model.
Inspect the two-hour SOC and power and compare with the source’s nominal-power scheduling abstraction.

checkpoints.label: Charge power tapers by two hours

modules.reflection: Why must the browser taper not be presented as a verified charging curve for a particular EV or as an EMHASS scheduling result?

modules.title: Reject an infeasible target before automation
modules.objective: Document an energy shortfall and preserve the planner/executor responsibility boundary.
steps: Use an 80 kWh battery at 30% SOC, 15 kW charger power, and 90% efficiency.
Test a two-hour target of 80% SOC and calculate why this window is insufficient.
Export the assumptions and read how the cookbook separates EMHASS planning from evcc execution.

checkpoints.label: Only 27 kWh are stored in the window
SOC remains below the requested 80% target

modules.reflection: What should a real automation do when a plan is infeasible or stale, and what evidence would you require before connecting an executor?
